questions.stem: Consider this: A plaintiff filing in federal court claims federal question jurisdiction. One party is a citizen of the same state. Which statement best states the governing legal rule?

options.text: A defendant's federal defence creates federal question jurisdiction in the case at hand.
options.misconception: treats a federal defence as enough

options.text: Federal question jurisdiction requires parties from different states on this record.
options.misconception: confuses federal question with diversity

options.text: Federal question jurisdiction exists when the plaintiff's well-pleaded complaint presents a claim arising under federal law, not merely when a federal issue might arise as a defence in the case at hand.
A case belongs in federal court whenever a federal statute is mentioned anywhere in this situation.
options.misconception: assumes any federal issue suffices

questions.explanation: The well-pleaded complaint rule keeps the analysis focused on the plaintiff's claim. A federal issue that appears only in a defence or in an expected reply does not make the case one arising under federal law. Here the decisive point is federal question jurisdiction, so the result follows from that doctrine rather than from the surface appeal of a competing statement. Each distractor rests on a different mistake about how the doctrine operates.
questions.hint: Read the complaint, not the anticipated defence. Keep the inquiry on federal question jurisdiction.
